t: There are 118 elements. Humans picked this one to be money.
Why this one? Let's run the tournament.
Round one: gases. Open your wallet, and your savings float away.
Liquids are out too. Mercury money slips through your fingers, and it's toxic.
Next, the hotheads. Sodium and potassium react violently with water. Good luck on a rainy payday.
Radioactive elements? Your wallet would glow. So would you.
Iron rusts. Money that rots in your pocket? Out, along with most of the table.
Some metals are just too rare to go around. Rhodium wasn't even discovered until 1804.
That leaves the final three: platinum, silver, and gold.
Platinum melts at nearly 1,800 degrees Celsius. No ancient furnace came close.
Silver was money for centuries too, but it tarnishes black.
Gold melts in a simple furnace, never rusts, and is rare, but not too rare.
Tutankhamun's mask still shines after 3,300 years.
Why so rare? Much of it was likely forged when two dead stars collided.
All the gold ever mined would fit in one cube, about 22 meters on each side.
117 elements tried out. Only one became money.
